# Playbook: Ref Commons (Fishery)

**When the stock is high and stable (roughly the same as last season) and other boats are taking their sustainable share, I take slightly above the sustainable share — about 10–20% more.** The regrowth absorbs the small deficit and I bank extra fish each season at minimal cost.

**When the stock has dropped sharply (e.g., others overfished), I immediately recalibrate to the new sustainable share of the reduced stock.** I do not try to "make up" lost fish by overfishing a diminished stock; that accelerates the decline and shrinks every future season.

**In the final season, I take a large fraction of the remaining stock — around 60–80% divided among boats, or simply a number well above sustainable.** I only hold back enough to avoid driving the stock to zero (which would zero out my catch). There is no future to preserve.

**When I observe other boats consistently taking less than the sustainable share, I can afford to take more.** The stock will hold or grow, giving me room to extract extra without long-term cost.

**When I observe other boats taking more than the sustainable share, I pull back to the sustainable share or below.** I let them deplete the stock while I conserve my option value in later seasons.

**I never take more than my share of the current stock.** If the stock is S and there are N boats, I never exceed S/N in any single season, because a zero stock ends everything.

**I track the gap between the stock's actual trajectory and the sustainable trajectory each season.** If the stock is declining despite my taking the sustainable share, others are overfishing and I should stay at or below sustainable to preserve my later seasons. If the stock is stable or growing while I take above sustainable, I have room to keep pushing a bit higher.

# Playbook

**Final season:** Take a large fraction of the remaining stock — aim for roughly 40–50% of what's left. There is no future penalty. The only real constraint is the stock itself; if you take more than what's available you may not land it, so cap your submission at a number you're confident is within the stock after accounting for others' likely catches. Do not hover near the sustainable share.

**Earlier seasons (not the last):** Take about 1.2–1.5× the stated sustainable share. This banks extra above the cooperative baseline without pushing the stock toward collapse. The regrowth rule (50% of remainder) means a small overage each season is partially absorbed.

**If the stock is below roughly 60:** Drop to the sustainable share or slightly below. The buffer between "stock declines" and "stock hits zero" is thinner, and a collapse ends all future income.

**If the stock is near 100 (carrying capacity):** You can push toward the upper end of your 1.2–1.5× range, or a bit beyond, because regrowth from a high stock is generous.

**Read the other boats:** If prior seasons show others consistently taking well above sustainable, do not try to "save" the stock by dropping to the sustainable share yourself — the stock will decline regardless. Match their level or go slightly above it, and rely on the final-season overfishing for your big gain. If others are cooperative, your 1.2–1.5× multiplier is safe.

**Do not** take the exact sustainable share as a reflex. It is a floor, not a target. The sustainable share is the minimum that keeps the stock stable when *everyone* plays it; you benefit from taking a bit more because the regrowth mechanism absorbs small overages.

**Do not** be timid in the last season. The temptation to stay near sustainable because "the stock is healthy" is the main way to leave points on the table. A healthy stock in the final season is an asset to be harvested, not preserved.

# Playbook: ref_commons

**Core principle:** Your score is only your own total. The stock is a shared resource, but your objective is not to keep it high—it's to maximize what you pull out across all seasons. The "sustainable share" is the amount that keeps the stock flat; it is a floor for strategic thinking, not a ceiling.

**Final season:** This is where the real points are. When the last season is put to me, I take a large fraction of the stock—roughly the current stock minus what I estimate the other boats will take (use the sustainable share as a rough estimate of their pull). I do not hover near the sustainable share in the final round. The stock will drop to near zero; that does not matter because the game is over.

**Early seasons (first third):** I can take moderately above the sustainable share (1.5× to 2×) without serious harm, because the stock starts high and has a large buffer. This builds my total while the stock is resilient. I avoid taking more than 2.5× the sustainable share early, as that starts to erode the stock I'll want for later.

**Middle seasons:** I settle near or just slightly above the sustainable share. The purpose of the middle is to preserve enough stock for my final-season grab. I watch the stock trajectory: if it's dropping faster than I'd expect (others are overfishing), I pull back toward or even below the sustainable share to keep the fishery alive for my endgame. If the stock is stable or growing, I can stay at or slightly above sustainable.

**When the stock is declining and there are 2+ seasons left:** I drop to the sustainable share or below. My priority shifts to protecting the stock so my final-season catch is large. A small concession in the middle buys a much larger payoff at the end.

**When I see others catching well below sustainable:** I have room to take more. The stock will hold up, so I can push closer to 1.5× sustainable in middle seasons without risk.

**When I see others catching well above sustainable:** I tighten up. If the stock is being drained, I take only the sustainable share (or less) to avoid being the one who pushes it to zero and forfeits my own future seasons.

**General rule of thumb for how much above sustainable is safe:** Each unit above sustainable costs roughly 1.5 units of stock. Over the remaining seasons, I should not let the projected stock drop below about 30% of the initial stock before the final round, so I still have something substantial to take in the endgame.
